full_description: AI is becoming part of the technology children see every day. machine_learning_experiment_protocol.heading: 13-Step Machine Learning Experiment Protocol
steps: 1. Define the Question: Choose an achievable binary classification goal (e.g. pencil vs. eraser)
2. Choose Safe Classes: Select two distinct, non-personal categories
3. Choose Data: Select approved physical objects, classroom stationery, or drawings
4. Collect Training Examples: Capture varied positions and angles without personal identifiers
5. Label: Place each training example accurately into its corresponding class
6. Train: Run the browser-based training algorithm in Google Teachable Machine
7. Test on New Examples: Introduce previously unseen objects, positions, or backgrounds
8. Record Results: Document actual label, predicted label, correctness, and confidence
9. Identify a Limitation: Pinpoint incorrect predictions (e.g. background colour shortcut)
10. Improve Data: Add balanced variation, fix mislabeled items, and eliminate background bias
11. Retrain: Re-run model training with the improved, clean dataset
12. Retest: Evaluate the updated model on held-out test examples
13. Explain: Student explains the experiment, what failed, what improved, and why human review is essential

child_safety_policy.heading: Privacy-First Data Design & Child Safety Standard
child_safety_policy.approved_copy: Nova Skills enforces a strict child-safety standard. Students learn AI through supervised experiments using objects, drawings and approved non-personal datasets. Private learning activities are the default, and children are not required to publish models or submit facial and voice data.
prohibited_data_types: Child facial images, webcam headshots, or student photos
Facial expression labeling or emotion-detection datasets
Student voice recordings or audio identity samples
Full names, student IDs, home addresses, phone numbers, or school uniforms
Public project sharing, social AI profile creation, or public model hosting
safe_data_types: Toys and game pieces (toy cars, wooden blocks, dice)
Hand-drawn shapes, geometric figures, and color cards
Teacher-approved educational stock object image sets

information_verification_framework.heading: STOP → CHECK → COMPARE → CORRECT → EXPLAIN Framework

steps.description: Do not immediately accept an AI response as true simply because it sounds confident
Identify specific factual claims, names, dates, numbers, or scientific assertions
Look up reputable educational sources, reference books, or official institutions
Rewrite unsupported, misleading, or hallucinated claims with verified facts
Describe why the AI may have made the error and how the verified source confirms truth

portfolio.title: AI Explorer & Responsible Machine Learning Portfolio
portfolio.description: Four structured, teacher-supervised project deliverables demonstrating conceptual AI understanding, hands-on classifier experimentation, factual verification, and responsible digital citizenship.

deliverables.title: Object Classification Experiment
deliverables.description: A supervised machine learning classification experiment trained on at least two distinct, non-personal object categories (e.g. pencil vs. eraser, or toy car vs. block) using Google Teachable Machine.
deliverables.evidence: Experiment description, class definitions, sample training images, model predictions, and teacher observation log.

deliverables.title: Test-and-Improve Record
deliverables.description: A documented testing protocol using held-out, unseen test examples. Identifies at least one prediction failure or uncertainty, analyzes the cause (e.g. lighting or background shortcuts), makes a reasoned training data change, and retests.
deliverables.evidence: Initial test table, error analysis notes, dataset adjustments made, retrained model results, and comparative reflection.

deliverables.title: AI Output vs Human Verification
deliverables.description: A structured fact-checking exercise applying the STOP-CHECK-COMPARE-CORRECT-EXPLAIN framework to an AI-generated or teacher-supplied explanation, verifying claims against authoritative educational references.
deliverables.evidence: Original AI text, list of factual claims, authoritative source citations, highlighted discrepancies, and corrected human explanation.

deliverables.title: Original AI Literacy Presentation
deliverables.description: A child-friendly, multi-slide or poster presentation explaining how the experiment worked, why machine learning makes mistakes, how training data shapes predictions, and what responsible AI use means.
deliverables.evidence: Student presentation slides/poster, test result charts, safety guidelines, and live private walkthrough for parents/teachers.

assessment_model.title: AI Literacy & Responsible Machine Learning Assessment Rubric

breakdown.description: Explains algorithms vs machine learning, models, training examples, and everyday AI applications in clear language
Accurate class selection, appropriate labeling, safe non-personal data collection, and successful Teachable Machine training
Thorough testing on unseen examples, objective error identification, reasoned diagnosis of shortcuts, and meaningful retraining
Applying fact-checking methods to AI claims, demonstrating privacy awareness, bias recognition, and copyright respect
Clear, confident presentation of the experiment, honest discussion of model limitations, and reflective parent demonstration

criteria: Student explains concepts in their own words rather than repeating technical jargon
Strict adherence to child safety: zero personal facial images, voice recordings, or private data
Honest testing and analysis: recognizing and documenting incorrect predictions without fabricating accuracy
Methodical application of the STOP-CHECK-COMPARE-CORRECT-EXPLAIN verification protocol
Demonstration of respectful digital citizenship and understanding of human accountability
unacceptable_criteria: Uploading child facial images, recording voices, or attempting emotion recognition
Claiming a toy classroom classifier is 100% accurate or ready for commercial deployment
Fabricating test failures or claiming unverified accuracy metrics
Submitting AI-generated presentation text without student comprehension or verification
Publishing public model links or student profiles on open social platforms
